question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

PROSAIC
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Commonplace.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prosaic (adjective) means dull, ordinary and lacking imagination; matter-of-fact rather than poetic. (नीरस, साधारण)
◦ Example: The explanation turned out to be entirely prosaic — a loose wire.

 

• Commonplace carries the same sense — ordinary, unremarkable, met with every day. (सामान्य)
◦ Example: What was once a rare sight has become commonplace.

 

• The word is simply the adjective of prose, as opposed to verse. Prose is plain and unadorned; hence prosaic came to mean anything lacking beauty or imagination.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Poetic (काव्यात्मक): having the beauty or expressiveness of poetry — the direct opposite of prosaic.

 

• Option 2: Imaginative (कल्पनाशील): showing creativity and invention — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Inspired (प्रेरित, उत्कृष्ट): of outstanding quality, as if guided by inspiration — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the design: three antonyms and one synonym. Fix the meaning of the given word first, then discard every option that agrees with the majority sense.

 

• Other synonyms of prosaic: mundane, pedestrian, humdrum, banal, workaday, uninspired.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To let sleeping dogs lie
option_1: To avoid reviving an old quarrel or problem
option_2: To ignore a danger that is plainly visible
option_3: To rest thoroughly before a difficult task
option_4: To keep a secret even from close friends
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To avoid reviving an old quarrel or problem.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To let sleeping dogs lie" means to leave a settled matter alone, because raising it again would only cause fresh trouble. (पुराने झगड़े को न छेड़ना)
◦ Example: The dispute was finally forgotten, so it is wiser to let sleeping dogs lie.

 

• The image is straightforward: a sleeping dog is harmless, but a dog woken suddenly may bite. The idiom therefore counsels prudent silence, not cowardice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes wilful blindness, for which the idiom would be "to turn a blind eye" or "to bury one's head in the sand" — the commonest trap here.

 

• Option 3 takes the idiom literally as advice about rest.

 

• Option 4 describes secrecy, nearer to "to keep something under one's hat".

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of caution: "Don't rock the boat", "Don't stir up a hornet's nest", "To open a can of worms" (to start something that creates fresh complications) and "To leave well alone".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

ABATE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Intensify.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abate (verb) means to become less intense or widespread; to lessen or subside. It is used of storms, pain, fever, anger and noise. (कम होना, घटना)
◦ Example: The storm abated towards midnight and the boats returned.

 

• Its true opposite is intensify — to become or make stronger and more extreme. (तीव्र होना)
◦ Example: The search intensified after the second report came in.

 

• Note the legal and financial use of abate as well: a tax abatement is a reduction in the amount payable.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Diminish (घटना): to make or become less — a direct synonym.

 

• Option 2: Subside (शांत होना): to become less intense or to sink to a lower level — also a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Wane (क्षीण होना): to decrease in strength or extent, as the moon does after the full moon — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of abate: augment, escalate, aggravate, amplify, heighten.

 

• Useful pair: wax and wane — to increase and decrease. The moon waxes to the full and wanes to the new.

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Committment.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Commitment" — a pledge or obligation, or dedication to a cause. (प्रतिबद्धता)
◦ Example: The department reaffirmed its commitment to clearing pending files.

 

• Spelling key: COM + MIT + MENT. The verb commit doubles its final t before -ed and -ing (committed, committing) because the stress falls on the last syllable. Before the suffix -ment, however, no doubling occurs, since -ment begins with a consonant.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Grievance (शिकायत) — correctly spelt; note the "ie", as in grieve.

 

• Option 3: Acknowledgement (प्राप्ति-सूचना) — correctly spelt; the form acknowledgment without the middle e is also accepted, chiefly in American usage.

 

• Option 4: Extravagance (फजूलखर्ची) — correctly spelt, ending in "-ance".

 

NOTE

 

• The same rule governs other -ment words: equipment, judgement, enrolment (British) and fulfilment (British) all keep a single consonant before the suffix. Compare commitment with committed and committee, both of which do take the double t.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the synthetic polymer widely used as a non-stick coating on cookware.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Polytetrafluoroethylene.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Polytetrafluoroethylene", abbreviated PTFE, is the synthetic polymer used as a non-stick coating on cookware and as a low-friction lining in industry. (नॉन-स्टिक लेप में प्रयुक्त बहुलक)
◦ Example: The pan is coated with polytetrafluoroethylene, so very little oil is needed.

 

• Break the word into its parts: POLY (many) + TETRA (four) + FLUORO (fluorine) + ETHYLENE (the base molecule). Reading long chemical names segment by segment is the reliable method in such questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Polytetraflouroethylene" — incorrect; the element is fluorine, so the segment is "fluoro", not "flouro". This is the most frequent error of all.

 

• Option 2: "Polytetrafluroethylene" — incorrect; the "o" of fluoro has been dropped.

 

• Option 4: "Polytetrafluoroethelene" — incorrect; the ending is "-ethylene", with a y.

 

NOTE

 

• Other polymer names worth remembering for spelling: polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, polyurethane and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A person who endures pain or hardship without showing feeling or complaint'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Stoic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A stoic is a person who bears suffering and misfortune calmly, without complaint and without any outward display of feeling. (धीरजवान, सहनशील व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: She bore the long illness with a stoic silence that surprised everyone.

 

• The word comes from Stoicism, the school of Greek philosophy founded by Zeno, which taught that a wise person should remain undisturbed by pleasure or pain alike. The school met at the stoa, a covered colonnade in Athens, which gave it its name.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Cynic (निंदक, संशयी): one who believes that people are motivated purely by self-interest.

 

• Option 3: Sceptic (संदेहवादी): one who habitually doubts accepted opinions and asks for proof.

 

• Option 4: Hedonist (सुखवादी): one who regards pleasure as the chief good in life — in effect the opposite of a stoic.

 

NOTE

 

• Related one-word substitutes for temperament: Ascetic (one who abstains from all indulgence), Optimist, Pessimist, Misanthrope (a hater of mankind), Misogynist (a hater of women) and Altruist (one who lives for others).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The panel included five economists, three of ___ had served on earlier commissions.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. whom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank follows the preposition "of" and refers back to persons (five economists). After a preposition, the required relative pronoun for people is "whom".

◦ Structure: noun + quantifier + of + whom/which + verb.
◦ Example: He wrote to eleven officers, none of whom replied.

 

• The construction joins the two clauses into one sentence. Using "them" would leave two independent clauses spliced by a comma — a comma splice — which is a punctuation error.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: them — a personal pronoun, which cannot link a subordinate clause to the main clause.

 

• Option 2: which — correct in this structure, but only for animals and things: twelve files, three of which were missing.

 

• Option 4: those — a demonstrative, not a relative pronoun.

 

NOTE

 

• The same pattern works with all, both, many, several, most, none, some, half and a few: the delegates, most of whom were first-timers; the buildings, many of which need repair.

 

• Remember that "that" can never follow a preposition, so three of that is impossible in any context.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The two accounts of the incident are mutually ___; if one is true, the other cannot be.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. exclusive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Mutually exclusive" describes two things that cannot both be true or both occur at the same time — the acceptance of one rules out the other. (परस्पर अपवर्जी)
◦ Example: The two schemes are mutually exclusive; a candidate may claim only one.

 

• The clause after the semicolon — if one is true, the other cannot be — is a definition of the phrase, and settles the answer by itself.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: inclusive — would mean the two accounts can coexist, contradicting the second clause.

 

• Option 3: dependent — would mean each relies on the other, which is again the opposite of the sense required.

 

• Option 4: beneficial — mutually beneficial is a real phrase, but it describes an arrangement that helps both sides and has no bearing here.

 

NOTE

 

• Fixed phrases built on mutually: mutually exclusive, mutually beneficial, mutually agreed, mutually intelligible (of languages that speakers of each can understand).

 

• Other adverb–adjective collocations tested by SSC: diametrically opposed, patently false, utterly impossible, highly unlikely, wholly unacceptable and fully aware.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

By the time the relief team reached the village, the flood water ___ already receded.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Two past actions are described. The receding of the water happened before the team arrived, so the earlier action takes the past perfect and the later one the simple past.

◦ Structure: By the time + simple past, … had + V3.
◦ Correct: By the time the team reached the village, the water had already receded.

 

• The adverb "already" is a further pointer: it is normally used with a perfect tense, and its position between the auxiliary and the participle is exactly what the sentence requires.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: has — the present perfect cannot be used in a wholly past narration.

 

• Option 2: would have — belongs to a conditional sentence, and no condition is present here.

 

• Option 3: was — was receded is not a possible form, since recede is intransitive and has no passive.

 

NOTE

 

• Expressions that regularly signal a past perfect: by the time, before, after, no sooner … than, hardly … when, already, till then and as soon as. In each case, ask which of the two actions finished first — that one takes had + V3.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The climate of Bengaluru (1)/ is far better than Chennai (2)/ in the months (3)/ between April and June. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of incomplete or illogical comparison. As written, the sentence compares the climate of Bengaluru with Chennai — that is, a climate with a city. Only like things may be compared.

◦ Corrected sentence: The climate of Bengaluru is far better than that of Chennai in the months between April and June.
◦ Or: Bengaluru has a far better climate than Chennai …

 

• The repair is made with "that of" for a singular noun and "those of" for a plural one.

◦ Example: The rates of this bank are lower than those of its competitors.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the climate of Bengaluru is a well-formed noun phrase.

 

• Part (3) is correct — in the months rightly takes in for a period of time.

 

• Part (4) is correct — between April and June uses the standard between … and pair.

 

NOTE

 

• The same fault appears in sentences such as The population of Mumbai is greater than Pune (→ than that of Pune) and Her handwriting is neater than her sister (→ than her sister's). Always ask: which two things are actually being compared?

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The committee only recommended (1)/ two of the eleven proposals (2)/ that had been submitted (3)/ before the last date. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is a misplaced modifier. The adverb "only" must be placed immediately before the word it limits. As written, only recommended suggests that the committee did nothing except recommend — it did not, say, approve or reject.

 

• The intended meaning is that the number recommended was small, so only belongs before "two".

◦ Corrected sentence: The committee recommended only two of the eleven proposals that had been submitted before the last date.

 

• Compare how the meaning shifts with position: Only the committee recommended two proposals / The committee only recommended two proposals / The committee recommended only two proposals. Each says something different.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct — two of the eleven proposals is properly formed.

 

• Part (3) is correct — the past perfect passive suits an action completed before the recommendation.

 

• Part (4) is correct — before the last date is a well-formed adverbial.

 

NOTE

 

• The same rule governs just, even, merely, almost, nearly, hardly and also. Each must stand next to the word it qualifies:
◦ He almost finished the paper (he did not finish) versus He finished almost the whole paper.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The workers are repairing the boundary wall of the school.
option_1: The boundary wall of the school was being repaired by the workers.
option_2: The boundary wall of the school has been repaired by the workers.
option_3: The boundary wall of the school is being repaired by the workers.
option_4: The boundary wall of the school is repaired by the workers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The boundary wall of the school is being repaired by the workers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Present Continuous Tense — structure: is/are + V-ing.

 

• The passive of the present continuous is formed as: Object + is/are being + V3 + by + Subject.

◦ Active: The workers are repairing the boundary wall.
◦ Passive: The boundary wall is being repaired by the workers.

 

• The auxiliary agrees with the new subject: the boundary wall is singular, so "is being" is used, not are being.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses "was being repaired", the passive of the past continuous, shifting the action into the past.

 

• Option 2 uses "has been repaired", the passive of the present perfect, which presents the work as finished.

 

• Option 4 uses "is repaired", the passive of the simple present, which states a habitual fact rather than an action in progress.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive forms of the continuous group: Present Continuous → is/are being + V3; Past Continuous → was/were being + V3. The future continuous and all perfect continuous tenses have no passive form in ordinary use.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The foundation stone of the bridge was laid by the Chief Minister in 1998.
option_1: The Chief Minister laid the foundation stone of the bridge in 1998.
option_2: The Chief Minister had laid the foundation stone of the bridge in 1998.
option_3: The Chief Minister has laid the foundation stone of the bridge in 1998.
option_4: The foundation stone of the bridge laid the Chief Minister in 1998.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The Chief Minister laid the foundation stone of the bridge in 1998.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Simple Past Passive — structure: was/were + V3. Its active counterpart is the Simple Past Active — V2.

◦ Passive: The foundation stone was laid by the Chief Minister.
◦ Active: The Chief Minister laid the foundation stone.

 

• In the conversion the agent after "by" becomes the subject, the original subject becomes the object, and the tense is preserved. The date 1998 confirms that a simple past is required, since a finished past time cannot take a perfect tense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses the past perfect, which would require a second, later past action for reference.

 

• Option 3 uses the present perfect, which cannot be combined with a definite past time such as in 1998.

 

• Option 4 reverses the roles — the foundation stone becomes the doer.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the forms of the verb: lay – laid – laid (transitive, to place something down) as against lie – lay – lain (intransitive, to recline). Only lay has a passive, which is why was laid is correct here.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The engineers inspected the site proposed for the new bus depot.
option_1: The site chosen for the depot lies beyond the canal.
option_2: Surveyors visited the site again last week.
option_3: The site was cleared well before the monsoon.
option_4: Counsel was asked to cite the relevant judgment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Counsel was asked to cite the relevant judgment.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Site is a noun meaning a place or location, especially one set aside for a building or an event.
• Cite is a verb meaning to quote or refer to something as evidence or authority. The two are pronounced alike, so "cite" is the homophone required.

◦ Example: The judgment cited three earlier rulings of the High Court.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all reuse the same spelling "site" in the same sense of a location, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• This family has a third member: sight, meaning the faculty of seeing or a thing seen. Keep all three apart — the site of the fort, he cited the rule, a magnificent sight.

 

• Related noun forms: citation from cite, and sighting from sight.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

India's transformation into the world's largest producer of milk began not with a technology but with a grievance. In 1946 the dairy farmers of Kaira district in Gujarat, tired of selling to a single contractor who fixed the price as he pleased, formed a cooperative of their own and refused to supply him. The union they built at Anand established a principle that would shape the sector for the rest of the century: the producer, and not the middleman, should own the processing and the marketing.

 

For two decades the model remained a local success. It was scaled nationally only in 1970, when the National Dairy Development Board launched Operation Flood, a programme that linked village cooperatives to city markets through a chain of chilling plants, transport and processing units. The design borrowed very little from the dairy technology of the West. What it took instead was an organisational insight — that a smallholder with two animals could compete with a large farm provided collection, testing and payment were made routine and daily.

 

The results were substantial rather than miraculous. Milk output rose from about 22 million tonnes in 1970 to more than three times that figure by the end of the century, and India passed the United States as the largest producer in 1998. Payment reached the household directly, and because the animals were usually tended by women, a significant share of it reached them.

 

The programme's limits are as instructive as its achievements. Yield per animal in India remains low by international standards, and the gains were uneven across states, concentrated where cooperative institutions were already strong. What Operation Flood demonstrated was not that milk is easy to produce, but that an ownership structure can accomplish what a subsidy cannot.

 

In which year was Operation Flood launched?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 1970.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second paragraph states that the Anand model was scaled nationally only in 1970, when the National Dairy Development Board launched Operation Flood.

 

• The passage supplies four dates, and each belongs to a different event. Keeping them apart is the whole task in this question:

◦ 1946 — the Kaira farmers form their cooperative.
◦ 1970 — Operation Flood is launched.
◦ 1998 — India passes the United States as the largest producer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: 1946 is the year the cooperative was formed at Kaira, two decades before the national programme.

 

• Option 3: 1980 appears nowhere in the passage.

 

• Option 4: 1998 is the year India became the largest milk producer, an outcome of the programme rather than its start.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage is dense with dates, mark each one against its event before looking at the options. SSC builds distractors precisely out of the other correct dates in the passage.

What prompted the dairy farmers of Kaira to form a cooperative of their own?
option_1: A sudden collapse in the demand for milk
option_2: A government order requiring them to organise
option_3: The arrival of new dairy technology from the West
option_4: Dependence on a single contractor who fixed the price as he pleased
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Dependence on a single contractor who fixed the price as he pleased.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first paragraph states it directly: the farmers were tired of selling to a single contractor who fixed the price as he pleased, and so formed a cooperative and refused to supply him.

 

• The author's opening sentence frames the whole passage around this point — the transformation began not with a technology but with a grievance. The problem was one of bargaining power, not of production.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 invents a collapse in demand that the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 2 reverses the story — the initiative came from the farmers themselves, and the state programme followed twenty-four years later.

 

• Option 3 is contradicted by the second paragraph, which says the design borrowed very little from Western dairy technology.

 

NOTE

 

• The opening sentence of a passage often states the author's thesis in compressed form. Here "not with a technology but with a grievance" anticipates both this answer and the conclusion in the last paragraph.

• The second paragraph names it plainly: in 1970 the National Dairy Development Board launched Operation Flood, a programme linking village cooperatives to city markets through chilling plants, transport and processing units.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

• Option 2 names the original union of 1946, which built the model but did not launch the national programme.

 

• Options 3 and 4 name bodies that do not appear in the passage at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Questions naming an institution, scheme or programme are pure location questions — the answer is a proper noun sitting in the text. Read the sentence containing the scheme's name and the agency is almost always in the same clause.

What does the author observe about the way the gains of the programme were distributed?
option_1: They were shared equally across all the states
option_2: They accrued mainly to large commercial farms
option_3: They were uneven, concentrated where cooperative institutions were already strong
option_4: They were confined entirely to the state of Gujarat
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They were uneven, concentrated where cooperative institutions were already strong.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The last paragraph states that the gains were uneven across states, concentrated where cooperative institutions were already strong, and pairs this with the observation that yield per animal remains low by international standards.

 

• The remark supports the author's larger claim. If the programme worked best where cooperatives already existed, then what mattered was the institutional structure, not the money or the technology — which is exactly the conclusion drawn in the final sentence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 contradicts the word "uneven".

 

• Option 2 reverses the design of the scheme, which was built around the smallholder with two animals.

 

• Option 4 overstates the limitation; the passage says the gains were concentrated, not confined to one state.

 

NOTE

 

• Note how the author opens the paragraph: "The programme's limits are as instructive as its achievements." A sentence of that kind announces that criticism is coming, and the questions built on such paragraphs almost always ask what the limits were.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

India's transformation into the world's largest producer of milk began not with a technology but with a grievance. In 1946 the dairy farmers of Kaira district in Gujarat, tired of selling to a single contractor who fixed the price as he pleased, formed a cooperative of their own and refused to supply him. The union they built at Anand established a principle that would shape the sector for the rest of the century: the producer, and not the middleman, should own the processing and the marketing.

 

For two decades the model remained a local success. It was scaled nationally only in 1970, when the National Dairy Development Board launched Operation Flood, a programme that linked village cooperatives to city markets through a chain of chilling plants, transport and processing units. The design borrowed very little from the dairy technology of the West. What it took instead was an organisational insight — that a smallholder with two animals could compete with a large farm provided collection, testing and payment were made routine and daily.

 

The results were substantial rather than miraculous. Milk output rose from about 22 million tonnes in 1970 to more than three times that figure by the end of the century, and India passed the United States as the largest producer in 1998. Payment reached the household directly, and because the animals were usually tended by women, a significant share of it reached them.

 

The programme's limits are as instructive as its achievements. Yield per animal in India remains low by international standards, and the gains were uneven across states, concentrated where cooperative institutions were already strong. What Operation Flood demonstrated was not that milk is easy to produce, but that an ownership structure can accomplish what a subsidy cannot.

 

What is implied by the closing sentence of the passage?
option_1: That subsidies should be withdrawn from all agricultural programmes
option_2: That how producers are organised can matter more than how much money is spent
option_3: That milk production is technically simple and needs no expertise
option_4: That cooperatives should replace private enterprise in every sector
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That how producers are organised can matter more than how much money is spent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage ends by stating that Operation Flood demonstrated not that milk is easy to produce, but that an ownership structure can accomplish what a subsidy cannot.

 

• The contrast is between two kinds of intervention — money transferred (a subsidy) and ownership rearranged (a cooperative). The author's claim is that the second proved the more powerful, which is precisely what Option 2 restates.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 pushes the argument much further than the author does; nowhere is the withdrawal of subsidies recommended.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the sentence directly — the author expressly denies that milk is easy to produce.

 

• Option 4 generalises a claim about one sector into a doctrine about all of them.

 

NOTE

 

• In implication questions the correct option restates the author's point in different words and stops where the author stops. Options that extend the argument into a sweeping policy prescription are the standard trap.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

She prefers reading than watching television in the evening.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. prefers reading to watching.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "prefer" is followed by "to", never by than, when two things are being compared.

◦ Corrected sentence: She prefers reading to watching television in the evening.
◦ Example: Most candidates prefer the morning shift to the afternoon one.

 

• The two items compared must also be in the same form — here both are gerunds, reading and watching.

 

• With infinitives, the pattern changes: prefer takes "rather than", as in I would prefer to walk rather than to wait for the bus.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original error.

 

• Option 2 mixes an infinitive with a gerund and keeps the wrong than.

 

• Option 4 uses the plural verb "prefer" with the singular subject She, besides retaining than.

 

NOTE

 

• Words taking "to" rather than than: prefer, preferable, superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior. Note also that preferable is never used with more.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

He behaves as if he was the owner of the entire building.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. as if he were.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "As if" and "as though" introduce an imaginary or unreal comparison. In such clauses the verb be takes the subjunctive form "were" for every subject, singular or plural.

◦ Corrected sentence: He behaves as if he were the owner of the entire building.
◦ Example: She speaks as if she were in charge of the department.

 

• The sense is decisive: he is not the owner. Where the supposition might actually be true, ordinary tenses are used — It looks as if it is going to rain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "as if he was" uses the ordinary past, which does not express an unreal situation.

 

• Option 2: "as if he is" treats an untrue supposition as a fact.

 

• Option 3: "as if he has been" introduces a perfect tense with no basis in the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• Other structures taking the unreal past: "I wish I were…", "If only he were here…", "It is high time we left…", "Suppose we were to accept…" and "would rather you came…" In each, a past form carries a present or future meaning.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The clerk said, "I must finish the reconciliation today."
option_1: The clerk said that he must finish the reconciliation that day.
option_2: The clerk said that he had to finish the reconciliation that day.
option_3: The clerk said that he must have finished the reconciliation that day.
option_4: The clerk said that he has to finish the reconciliation today.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The clerk said that he had to finish the reconciliation that day.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, so the reported clause is backshifted. Three changes are needed:

◦ Modal: must, when it expresses obligation, becomes "had to".
◦ Pronoun: I becomes he.
◦ Time word: today becomes "that day".

 

• Applying all three together gives Option 2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps "must" unchanged and so fails to backshift the modal.

 

• Option 3 uses "must have finished", which expresses a deduction about the past, not an obligation.

 

• Option 4 changes neither the tense nor the time word.

 

NOTE

 

• Modal changes in indirect speech: can → could; may → might; will → would; shall → should; must → had to. The modals could, would, should, might, ought to and used to remain unchanged.

 

• One exception: must stays must when it expresses a permanent truth or a strong general rule — He said that we must all die one day.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The engineer assured the residents that the repair would be completed before the festival.
option_1: "The repair will be completed before the festival," the engineer assured the residents.
option_2: "The repair would be completed before the festival," the engineer assured the residents.
option_3: "The repair is completed before the festival," said the engineer.
option_4: "The repair had been completed before the festival," the engineer assured the residents.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "The repair will be completed before the festival," the engineer assured the residents.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Converting back to direct speech reverses the ordinary rules of backshift. Since the reporting verb assured is in the past, the reported "would" must be restored to its original form "will".

◦ Indirect: … assured the residents that the repair would be completed …
◦ Direct: "The repair will be completed …"

 

• The words are then enclosed in inverted commas, the conjunction that is dropped, and the reporting verb assured is retained, since it names the manner of speaking.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 leaves "would" inside the quotation, so the backshift has not been undone.

 

• Option 3 changes the tense to the simple present, altering the meaning to a habitual fact.

 

• Option 4 uses the past perfect, which would mean the repair was already finished before the promise was made.

 

NOTE

 

• Reverse changes when moving from indirect to direct speech: would → will; could → can; might → may; had to → must; that day → today; the next day → tomorrow; the previous day → yesterday; there → here.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Until a few years ago the hamlet of Sonpura appeared on no official map of the district.

 

A. Letters for its residents were therefore delivered to a village four kilometres away.

 

B. He walked its lanes on his rest days and drew each one on a sheet of graph paper.

 

C. A postman named Iqbal, weary of the daily detour, decided to settle the matter himself.

 

D. The revenue office accepted his sketch after verifying it on the ground and issued Sonpura a survey number.

 

S2. The hamlet has had a postal address of its own, and a bus stop to go with it, ever since.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A-C-B-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – C – B – D – S2. The paragraph follows a situation → consequence → initiative → action → outcome order.

 

• S1 states the situation — the hamlet is on no map.

◦ A gives the consequence, and the word "therefore" ties it directly to S1: letters went to another village.
◦ C introduces the initiative, and it must precede B because "He" in B can refer to nobody but the postman named here. Note too that C's phrase the daily detour looks back to the delivery arrangement in A.
◦ B is his action — walking the lanes and drawing the map.
◦ D gives the outcome, and "his sketch" refers to the graph paper of B.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-A-B-D) introduces the daily detour before the detour has been described.

 

• Option 3 (A-B-C-D) lets "He" appear before the postman has been named.

 

• Option 4 (C-B-A-D) strands sentence A after the map has already been drawn.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence beginning with "therefore", "so", "as a result" or "consequently" states a consequence and must follow its cause. Spotting therefore in A fixes it immediately after S1 and eliminates half the options at once.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. A pair of noise-cancelling headphones does not muffle sound; it adds more of it.

 

A. A tiny speaker then plays that inverted wave into the ear alongside the original noise.

 

B. A microphone on the outer shell first samples the sound arriving from the surroundings.

 

C. Where a peak of one wave meets a trough of the other, the two cancel and the ear registers quiet.

 

D. Circuitry inside the earcup generates a second wave that is the exact mirror image of the first.

 

S2. The effect works best on the steady drone of an engine and least well on sudden speech.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2. The paragraph describes a process, and process paragraphs run in the order in which the stages occur.

 

• S1 states the paradox — the headphones add sound rather than blocking it.

◦ B is the first stage, and the word "first" marks it as such: the microphone samples the incoming noise.
◦ D follows B, since the "second wave" and "the first" presuppose a wave already captured.
◦ A follows D, because "that inverted wave" refers to the mirror image just generated.
◦ C is the result — the two waves cancel — and leads into the qualification in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (B-A-D-C) plays an inverted wave that has not yet been generated.

 

• Option 2 (D-B-A-C) generates a mirror image of a wave that has not yet been captured.

 

• Option 4 (A-B-D-C) opens with "that inverted wave", which has nothing to refer back to.

 

NOTE

 

• Two markers settle this question without any knowledge of acoustics: the ordinal word "first" in B fixes the opening, and the demonstrative "that" in A binds it to the sentence immediately before it.
